Demographic history of New York City :: By borough :: Brooklyn :: part 01 :: chunk_0007
In the early 1900s, Brooklyn was predominantly White, with the White population comprising 98.31% in 1900 and staying above 98% through 1920. The Black population was very small at this time, constituting only 1.57% in 1900, while the Asian population was even smaller at 0.11%.

The 1930s started to see a slight decline in the White population, dropping to 97.20%, and the Black population began to grow, reaching 2.69% by 1930. The Asian population remained negligible.

From the 1940s to the 1960s, the decline in the White population became more pronounced, dropping to 92.22% in 1950 and then to 85.48% in 1960. During this period, the Black population increased to 14.14%, and the Asian population began to grow, albeit slowly.

The 1970s and 1980s marked a significant shift in Brooklyn's demographics. The White population fell to 73.24% in 1970 and then sharply to 56.01% in 1980. The Black population increased to 25.22% in 1970 and 32.40% in 1980. The Asian community and Other or Mixed category became more substantial, reaching 1.93% and 9.67%, respectively, in 1980. The Hispanic/Latino community grew to 17.58%, and the foreign-born population remained relatively high, at 23.80% in 1980.

In the last three decades, from 1990 to 2010, Brooklyn's racial and ethnic diversity expanded further. The White population declined to below half of the total, reaching 42.80% in 2010, while the Black population remained around 34-37%. The Asian population increased significantly to 10.52% by 2010, and the Other or Mixed category reached 12.34%. The Hispanic/Latino population hovered around 19-20%, and the foreign-born population grew to 36.44% in 2010.

Kubala was born in [Budapest](/wiki/Budapest "Budapest"), as were his parents, who came from mixed backgrounds. His mother, Anna Stecz, a factory worker, had Polish and Slovak roots, while his father, Pál Kubala Kurjas, a bricklayer, was Slovak. Kubala described himself as a "[cosmopolitan](/wiki/Cosmopolitanism "Cosmopolitanism")". He began his career as a junior player with Ganz TE, a factory team that played in the Hungarian third division. At the age of 11, he was playing in teams with other players who were three to five years older.[[8]](#cite_note-8) At the age of 18, he signed for [Ferencvárosi](/wiki/Ferencv%C3%A1rosi_TC "Ferencvárosi TC") where he was a teammate of [Sándor Kocsis](/wiki/S%C3%A1ndor_Kocsis "Sándor Kocsis"). In 1946, Kubala moved to [Czechoslovakia](/wiki/Czechoslovakia "Czechoslovakia"), allegedly to avoid military service, and joined [Slovan Bratislava](/wiki/%C5%A0K_Slovan_Bratislava "ŠK Slovan Bratislava"). In 1947, he married Anna Viola Daučíkova, the sister of the Czechoslovak national coach, [Ferdinand Daučík](/wiki/Ferdinand_Dau%C4%8D%C3%ADk "Ferdinand Daučík"). In 1948, Kubala returned to Hungary, again to allegedly avoid military service, and joined [Vasas](/wiki/Vasas_SC "Vasas SC").

Songjeong beach facing south

Busan is called the summer capital of Korea[[49]](#cite_note-51) since it attracts tourists from all over the country to its six beaches. Luxury hotels and a carnival boardwalk line the beach at [Haeundae](/wiki/Haeundae_Beach "Haeundae Beach"). [Gwangalli Beach](/wiki/Gwangalli_Beach "Gwangalli Beach") has cafés, bars, and restaurants along the beach, and the Grand Gwangan Bridge. Other beaches include Dadaepo Beach on the west edge of the city and [Songdo Beach](/wiki/Songdo_Beach "Songdo Beach"), south of central Busan.

[Haeundae Beach](/wiki/Haeundae_Beach "Haeundae Beach") is Busan's most famous beach.[[50]](#cite_note-52) It is a staple setting for South Korean films and TV shows, such as the 2009 film *[Tidal Wave](/wiki/Tidal_Wave_(2009_film) "Tidal Wave (2009 film)")*. [Dongbaekseom](/wiki/Dongbaekseom "Dongbaekseom") is located at the southern end of [Haeundae Beach](/wiki/Haeundae_Beach "Haeundae Beach"). This island is picturesque with a thick forest of camellias and pine trees. Tourist attractions on Dongbaek Island include a walking path and the Nurimaru APEC House, built for the 2005 APEC summit. Songjeong beach is the next beach north of Haeundae Beach.

[Geumjeongsan](/wiki/Geumjeongsan "Geumjeongsan") to the west is a weekend hiking spot for Busan residents. To the north, the neighborhoods around [Pusan National University](/wiki/Pusan_National_University "Pusan National University") (also known as PNU, which is one of the most highly recognized national institutes of higher education in Korea) have student theaters, cafés, bars, and restaurants, as well as open-air cultural street performances on weekend nights. Nearby is [Beomeosa](/wiki/Beomeosa "Beomeosa"), the city's main [Korean Buddhist](/wiki/Korean_Buddhism "Korean Buddhism") temple.

The source of the [Blue Nile](/wiki/Blue_Nile "Blue Nile") is [Gish Abay](/wiki/Gish_Abay "Gish Abay") at the bottom of the bright line. The river flows north from there to [Lake Tana](/wiki/Lake_Tana "Lake Tana") at the top.

The longest course of the Nile – which includes the White Nile tributary – has several other tributaries. The drainage basins of the Blue Nile and the Atbarah comprise the final two regions of the Nile Basin.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHurst2025-12)

The Blue Nile springs from hills in Ethiopia where it originates as a stream named *Abay* near the town of [Gish Abay](/wiki/Gish_Abay "Gish Abay"): *Gish* is an [Amharic](/wiki/Amharic "Amharic") word meaning 'source', and Abay is the name of the stream.[[49]](#cite_note-63) Gish Abay flows into [Lake Tana](/wiki/Lake_Tana "Lake Tana"), a large, shallow lake, which has a single outflow where it adopts the "Blue Nile" name. The river then makes a wide loop: first south, then west through a spectacular gorge 2 kilometers (6,600 ft) deep, then north passing through South Sudan into Sudan, where it joins with the White Nile at Khartoum to form the main Nile.[[50]](#cite_note-64) Along its course, the Blue Nile generates electricity at several hydropower plants, including the [Tis Abay hydropower project](/w/index.php?title=Tis_Abay_hydropower_project&action=edit&redlink=1 "Tis Abay hydropower project (page does not exist)") at the [Blue Nile Falls](/wiki/Blue_Nile_Falls "Blue Nile Falls"), the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam near the border between Ethiopia and South Sudan, the [Roseires Dam](/wiki/Roseires_Dam "Roseires Dam") near the town of [Ad Damazin](/wiki/Ad_Damazin "Ad Damazin"), and the [Sennar Dam](/wiki/Sennar_Dam "Sennar Dam").[[51]](#cite_note-65) The size of the Blue Nile's drainage basin is over 306,000 square km.[[52]](#cite_
